lead: This unit explains how an axial member carries load: stress, strain, elastic constants, deformation, indeterminacy and thermal effects, ending with stored strain energy. After it you can find safe axial sizes, elongation of simple and compound bars, reactions in fixed-end bars, thermal stress, and maximum stress under sudden or impact load.
about: Chapter 1.1 defines normal and shear stress. 1.2 uses the tension test to read stress-strain curves. 1.3 states Hooke's law and factor of safety. 1.4 links E, G, K and Poisson's ratio, and 1.5 converts strains to volumetric strain. 1.6 computes axial deformation of simple and compound bars. 1.7 adds compatibility for statically indeterminate members. 1.8 puts temperature change into the same compatibility method. 1.9 closes with strain energy for gradual, sudden and impact loads. Each chapter uses the previous one: stress leads to strain, strain to deformation, deformation to compatibility, and compatibility to thermal and energy problems.

chapters.idea: Stress is internal force per unit area; normal stress acts perpendicular to a cut, shear stress acts along it.
chapters.depth: Rigid and deformable solids in one line. Axial force P (N), cross-section area A (m²), normal stress σ = P/A (Pa, or N/mm² = MPa). Use + for tension and − for compression. Average shear stress τ = V/A_s on a rivet, pin or cut face; V is shear force (N), A_s is shear area (m²). Stress is not force; units are N/m². Some syllabi call normal stress direct stress and shear stress tangential stress. Show a cut through a bar and the force on the cut face.

figure.title: From load to stress
figure.aria: An axial load is cut to expose internal force, which gives normal stress; a shear force on a face gives shear stress.

chapters.example: A 20 mm diameter steel rod carries an axial tensile load of 50 kN. Find the normal stress in the rod. Area = π/4 × (20 mm)² = 314.2 mm²; σ = 50000 N / 314.2 mm² = 159.2 N/mm² = 159.2 MPa.
chapters.trap: Using diameter as radius, or mixing mm² and m²; shear stress uses the shear area, not always the full cross-section.
chapters.leave: Oblique-plane stresses, principal stresses and Mohr's circle to Unit 2; beam bending and shear stress distributions to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: A tension test turns material behaviour into a stress-strain curve whose shape separates ductile from brittle materials.
chapters.depth: Engineering stress σ=P/A0 and engineering strain ε=ΔL/L0; gauge length L0. For mild steel: proportional limit, elastic limit, upper and lower yield, strain hardening, ultimate strength, necking, fracture. For brittle material: little plastic deformation, fracture near maximum. Define yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, breaking strength and percentage elongation. For no clear yield, some syllabi add the 0.2% offset proof stress. Young's modulus from the initial straight slope. Mention isotropic and homogeneous materials in one line. Do not derive true stress.

figure.aria: The mild-steel curve has a yield region and long plastic stretch; the cast-iron curve breaks with little plastic strain.

chapters.example: A mild steel specimen has gauge length 50 mm and diameter 10 mm. It yields at 18 kN, reaches an ultimate load of 35 kN, and the fractured gauge length is 62 mm. Find yield stress, ultimate stress and percentage elongation. A0 = 78.54 mm²; yield stress = 18000/78.54 = 229.2 MPa; ultimate stress = 35000/78.54 = 445.6 MPa; elongation = (62−50)/50 × 100 = 24%.
chapters.trap: Using the final area for engineering stress, or taking ultimate load as the breaking load; brittle materials have no yield plateau.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 1.1 for stress and strain definitions.
chapters.leave: Elastic constants and Poisson's ratio to 1.4; principal stresses and failure theories to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Within the elastic limit stress is proportional to strain; factor of safety turns a failure stress into a safe working stress.
chapters.depth: Hooke's law in tension σ=Eε; E is Young's modulus (Pa, GPa). In shear τ=Gγ; G is shear modulus or modulus of rigidity. State the elastic-limit condition. Factor of safety n = failure stress / allowable stress. Failure stress may be yield strength for ductile materials or ultimate strength for brittle materials, chosen by design. Allowable stress is also called working stress or permissible stress. Give reasons for FOS: load uncertainty, material variation, simplified analysis, consequences. No single universal FOS value.

figure.title: Factor of safety
figure.aria: The failure stress is divided by the factor of safety to give the working stress, which sets the safe axial load.

chapters.example: A mild steel tie rod has yield strength 250 MPa. Use a factor of safety 2.5. Find the allowable stress and the maximum axial load for a 12 mm diameter rod. σ_w = 250/2.5 = 100 MPa; A = π/4 × (12 mm)² = 113.1 mm²; P = 100 N/mm² × 113.1 mm² = 11.31 kN.
chapters.trap: Dividing the load by FOS instead of stress, or using ultimate strength for a ductile rod when design is based on yield.
chapters.leave: Detailed design codes and variable load factors are outside this unit.

chapters.idea: Four elastic constants E, G, K and ν describe an isotropic elastic material, and only two are independent.
chapters.depth: Define longitudinal strain ε and lateral strain ε_lat; Poisson's ratio ν = −ε_lat/ε (dimensionless). E is Young's modulus, G shear modulus or rigidity modulus, K bulk modulus. Relations: E = 2G(1+ν); E = 3K(1−2ν); E = 9KG/(3K+G). Isotropic and homogeneous materials. For isotropic elastic materials 0 ≤ ν ≤ 0.5; ν = 0.5 means incompressible (rubber-like ideal). Some syllabi call K modulus of volumetric elasticity. State relations; keep derivation short.

figure.aria: Node E sits at the centre, linked to G, K and ν by the standard elastic-constant relations.

chapters.trap: Using ν with the wrong sign, or putting K in place of G in E = 2G(1+ν); all moduli must use the same unit.
chapters.leave: Volumetric strain calculation to 1.5; 3D stress transformation to Unit 2.

chapters.idea: Volumetric strain is the fractional change in volume produced by the three normal strains.
chapters.depth: For a small element ε_v = ΔV/V = ε_x+ε_y+ε_z. Under uniaxial tension ε_x=σ/E and ε_y=ε_z=−νσ/E, so ε_v = σ/E (1−2ν). Under hydrostatic pressure p, ε_v = −p/K with K bulk modulus. Dilation is another name. Keep the small-strain assumption. For a bar, volume change ΔV = ε_v V0.

figure.title: Volumetric strain
figure.aria: Axial stress gives one extension strain and two lateral contraction strains; their sum is the volumetric strain.

chapters.example: A steel bar is under axial tensile stress 120 MPa. Take E = 200 GPa and ν = 0.30. Find the volumetric strain. ε = 120/200000 = 6×10⁻⁴; ε_v = 6×10⁻⁴ × (1−2×0.30) = 2.4×10⁻⁴ = 0.00024.
chapters.trap: Adding three equal axial strains, or forgetting the negative sign of lateral strains; ν = 0.5 gives zero volume change.
chapters.leave: Thin cylinder volume change to Unit 7; large deformation and plasticity outside this unit.

chapters.idea: Axial deformation is δ=PL/(AE); compound bars share load while bonded parts share the same strain.
chapters.depth: Derive δ for constant section; for a stepped bar δ=Σ P_i L_i/(A_i E_i). Bar of varying cross-section by integration δ=∫P dx/(A E). Compound bar of two materials in parallel: same strain ε, load P=P1+P2, σ1=E1ε, σ2=E2ε; find stresses. Composite sections. Principle of superposition for several axial loads in the linear elastic range. Some syllabi include self weight: δ=ρgL²/(2E)=WL/(2AE) for a uniform hanging bar. Keep fixed-end indeterminacy to chapter 7.

figure.title: Segments: L m, A mm², E GPa
figure.aria: Three rows list two stepped segments and their total; each segment contributes P L/(A E) to the extension.

chapters.example: A steel bar has two parts in series: part 1 length 0.4 m, area 300 mm²; part 2 length 0.6 m, area 200 mm². E=200 GPa and axial load is 40 kN. Find total elongation. δ1 = 40000×0.4/(300×10⁻⁶×200×10⁹)=0.267 mm; δ2 = 40000×0.6/(200×10⁻⁶×200×10⁹)=0.600 mm; total δ = 0.867 mm.
chapters.trap: Using total load for every segment of a stepped bar, or adding strains instead of elongations in a compound bar.
chapters.leave: Fixed-end reactions to 1.7; thermal strain to 1.8; beam deflection to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: When equilibrium alone cannot find axial reactions, compatibility of deformation supplies the extra equation.
chapters.depth: Define statically indeterminate: unknown reactions exceed equilibrium equations. For axial members use (1) equilibrium ΣF=0, (2) compatibility of elongations, (3) force-displacement δ=FL/(AE). Method of consistent deformations: remove a support, find free displacement, apply redundant reaction to cancel it. Bars fixed at both ends and parallel rods. Superposition allowed in the linear elastic range. Degree of indeterminacy = unknowns − equilibrium equations.

figure.title: Indeterminate axial bar
figure.aria: Equilibrium gives one equation, compatibility gives another, and the axial force-displacement relation lets us solve the reactions.

chapters.example: A prismatic bar of length 1.5 m and area 300 mm² is fixed at both ends. An axial load 30 kN is applied 0.5 m from the left end. Take E=200 GPa. Find the reactions at the two ends. R_L = P b/L = 30×1.0/1.5 = 20 kN; R_R = P a/L = 30×0.5/1.5 = 10 kN.
chapters.trap: Writing compatibility with the wrong sign, or using the full bar length for a segment; check that reactions add to the applied load.
chapters.leave: Thermal loading to 1.8; indeterminate beams to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: A temperature change wants to expand or contract a bar; restraint turns that free strain into thermal stress.
chapters.depth: Coefficient of thermal expansion α (1/K or 1/°C); free expansion δ_T=αLΔT. Fully restrained bar: σ = −EαΔT, compression on heating and tension on cooling. Partly restrained or composite bars: use compatibility δ_mechanical + δ_thermal = support movement and solve with equilibrium. Thermal strain ε_T=αΔT. For a bar with free ends thermal stress is zero. A temperature change in °C equals the change in K.

figure.title: Thermal stress
figure.aria: A temperature rise first causes free expansion; rigid supports prevent it and produce compressive thermal stress.

chapters.example: A steel bar 2 m long is fixed between rigid supports. E=200 GPa and α=12×10⁻⁶ /°C. Temperature rises by 50°C. Find the thermal stress. σ = EαΔT = 200×10⁹ × 12×10⁻⁶ × 50 = 120×10⁶ Pa = 120 MPa compression.
chapters.trap: Adding thermal expansion to mechanical elongation without a sign convention; using αLΔT as stress.
chapters.leave: Thermal stresses in beams and cylinders to later units; temperature-dependent properties outside this unit.

chapters.idea: Strain energy is the work stored in an elastic member; sudden and impact loads raise the maximum stress above the static value.
chapters.depth: Axial strain energy U = 1/2 Pδ = P²L/(2AE) = σ²/(2E) × volume. Gradual load: P rises from 0 to P, U=1/2Pδ. Suddenly applied constant load W: maximum stress 2W/A, maximum extension twice static, U = W δ_max. Impact by weight W falling height h: δ_max = δ_st[1+√(1+2h/δ_st)], σ_max = W/A[1+√(1+2h/δ_st)], with δ_st=WL/(AE). Shear strain energy U=τ²/(2G)×volume in one line. Some syllabi call strain energy resilience; proof resilience is U at the elastic limit.

figure.title: Load type and energy
figure.aria: Three load types branch from one node: gradual load gives half Pδ, sudden load doubles static extension, and impact load adds the drop height.

chapters.example: A vertical steel rod is 2 m long and has area 300 mm². E=200 GPa. A weight of 10 kN is suddenly applied to its lower end. Find maximum stress and maximum extension. Static stress = 10000/300 = 33.33 MPa; sudden maximum stress = 66.67 MPa. Static extension = 10000×2/(300×10⁻⁶×200×10⁹)=0.333 mm; sudden maximum extension = 0.667 mm.
chapters.trap: Using the gradual-load factor for a sudden load, or forgetting that the impact formula already includes the static extension.
chapters.leave: Strain energy in bending and torsion to Units 5 and 6; energy methods for deflection to Unit 5.
